docs.title: The CV pipeline
docs.text:
What POST /v1/cv does with the minutes it takes: six steps, each on a model of its own, then a render that trims the CV until it fits. The method is the one adapticv-ai worked out.

The code is src/pipeline_v1/cv_generator.py (CVGenerator, the steps as a LangGraph graph) with cv_review.py beside it (the validation loop), and two modules every pipeline shares, in src/common/: highlight.py (the highlighter) and cv_renderer.py (the compile and the page count).

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    START(["POST /v1/cv accepted<br/>202 + request_id"]) --> JD["<b>jd_evaluation</b><br/>the JD's key points, each with an importance"]
    JD -->|"Send, one per list"| SC["<b>profile_scoring</b><br/>one list of the profile against the key points"]
    SC --> MS["the scores into the profile<br/>text|3-80,7-40"]
    MS --> FS["<b>format_selection</b><br/>a format, the experiences, their duty caps"]
    FS -->|"Send"| WB["<b>cv</b><br/>the body"]
    FS -->|"Send, one per experience"| WD["<b>cv</b> (model <b>duties</b>)<br/>one experience"]
    WB --> CC["back in order"]
    WD --> CC
    CC -->|"Send"| VB["<b>validation</b><br/>the body, up to 5 rounds"]
    CC -->|"Send, one per experience"| VD["<b>validation</b><br/>one experience, up to 5 rounds"]
    VB --> CK["back in order"]
    VD --> CK
    CK --> HL["<b>highlight</b><br/>**bold** keywords, *italic* stacks"]
    HL --> R{"rendered:<br/>over the page limit?"}
    R -->|"yes, and a duty can go"| TRIM["remove the duty<br/>worth least"] --> R
    R -->|"no, or none can go"| FIN(["<b>result</b><br/>document · tex · pdf"])
Step Calls Shown Hands over jd_evaluation 1 the JD key_points: 6 to 15 requirements, each with keywords and an importance from 0 to 100 profile_scoring one per list of the profile — 9 for the example candidate the key points, one list, and its experience when the list is inside one scored_profile, score_reasons format_selection 1 the key points, the formats, the scored experiences format_selection: the format, the experiences shown, the duties of each, and why cv 1 for the body (model role cv), 1 per experience shown (model role duties) the key points, the writing style, the schema, the scored profile or experience, its duty cap and its evidence cv_body, cv_experiences validation 1 to 5 per document the writing style, the round, the profile or the experience without scores, the generated text, the replacements that failed checked_body, checked_experiences highlight 1 the key points, the CV the models wrote, the evidence highlighted_resume

Each step has its own role in models.toml; cv and validation each serve two prompts, the body's and the experiences'. Each step's result is streamed to the client as it is ready, and stored beside the CV under steps/.

Scores. profile_scoring gives every item of the profile the key points it matches, at most four, each scored 0–100 for how completely the item proves it: a string becomes Led the migration.|3-80,7-40 (key point 3 at 80, key point 7 at 40), an object gets a "score": "3-80,7-40" field. The words that prove each match stay out of the profile, in score_reasons; the writer and the highlighter are shown them as EVIDENCE. The scores ride along to the end and come off at the render.

Coverage. A key point counts its two best duty scores, up to twice its importance (COVERAGE_BEST, COVERAGE_CAP): a duty on a key point already covered adds nothing, and weak matches cannot fill a key point before its strong ones. The duties prompt says the same in words, and the trim below uses the same rule.

Formats. What format_selection chooses from:

Format Experiences Duties each Duties in all A 3 0–9 26 B 4 0–8 23 C 5 0–7 20

It fills the places with the duties that add the most coverage, keeping one or two for long duties the writer may split. Then it counts the years the chosen experiences cover: when a significant part of the career is missing, it moves to a format with more experiences and adds the longest one not shown, paying with the lowest-scoring duties. An experience with no duties shows only its role summary, which the writer turns into a synthesis of what you did there, under 180 characters.

The code assumes nothing about the CV or the profile beyond the work experiences (each with an id and its duties), their duties and the writing_style: the prompts and the template decide everything else.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
A step that makes several calls fans them out with LangGraph's Send: one node per profile list, per experience, and they run at the same time. Each writes its answer, tagged with its position, into a list the graph collects; a node in code puts the answers back in profile order before the next step starts. The steps themselves run one after another.

The parallel nodes run in the job's own context, so their log lines and their token counts land in the job's session like any other. A call that fails — three unusable replies, an endpoint that refuses — fails the job with its own cause and stage, after the calls beside it have finished.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The validators check facts and grammar against your profile, with minimal edits; style is the writers' business. Each violation comes back as a call of a tool — replace_in_body or replace_in_duties — which is only a schema: the code applies the replacement, in the order the calls came, and asks again. A round with no call ends the review. A replacement whose text is not found goes back to the model as a FAILED REPLACEMENT. After five rounds (MAX_VALIDATIONS) the CV goes on with the last edits: a CV with a doubtful line in it is worth more to you than an error.

The validators count no pages. The page limit is the render's business alone.

docs.title: The render
docs.text:
After the highlight the CV is rendered — your candidate_data merged over the top, the scores removed — and its pages are counted. While it runs past the page limit (pages, 2 by default), one duty goes: of the experiences with more than one duty, the duty whose removal loses the fewest coverage points; on a tie, the one with the lowest total score, then the older experience's. Then it is rendered again. When no duty can go, the longer CV is delivered.

Every render is of the merged document, so every page count is the page count of the CV you will send. That is why the endpoint takes candidate_data. No model is ever shown it: the highlighter sees what the models wrote, and your data goes over the top at the render, so a field a model invents can never replace a real name, email or address.

The renders before the last stay in the job's scratch directory. Only the final PDF is sent, in the result.

docs.title: Retries, limits and what each failure costs
docs.text:
Guard Limit Set by On exhaustion Calls per model request (empty, cut off, or not the JSON asked for) 3 ATTEMPTS in common/models/selector.py 502 model_output, except for the highlight Highlight the same the same a warning; the CV is delivered unmarked Validation rounds per document 5 MAX_VALIDATIONS in pipeline_v1/cv_review.py the CV goes on with the last edits One pdflatex compile 120 s ATS_LATEX_TIMEOUT 504 latex_timeout

A reply that is JSON is parsed and its type checked — a list or an object — and nothing more, as adapticv-ai does: no schema is enforced. A reply whose items do not line up with what was asked (fewer scores than items) fails the job.

docs.title: What the client sees while it runs
docs.text:
The job's session streams a status event as each step starts, with one line about the step that just finished: what it produced, and its tokens, thinking and time. Between them come an artifact event with each step's result, as the JSON it is, and the log and usage events that say what each model call did and cost.

{"status": "cv",
 "detail": "format A: experiences [0, 1, 2], duties [8, 8, 6], tokens used=4210, thinking=1952, elapsed=24.3s"}

The render belongs to the highlight step: it takes a second or a few.

The session ends with a result event — the document, its LaTeX and its PDF, and what the whole run cost — or, for a job that failed, an error event with the status and cause the work produced (502, 504, 422) and what it cost anyway. Either way it is the last thing the stream carries.

docs.title: Changing it for one request
docs.text:
Every prompt and both schemas the writer is shown can be replaced by a part of the same name: sys_prompt_jd_evaluation, sys_prompt_profile_scoring, sys_prompt_format_selection, sys_prompt_cv_body, cv_body_schema, sys_prompt_cv_duties, cv_duties_schema, sys_prompt_validation_body, sys_prompt_validation_duties, sys_prompt_highlight. So can the template and its images. The prompts and schemas are what the models read: editing one changes what they write.

Each step's model settings can be replaced too: <step>_extra_body, a JSON object, supersedes every setting models.toml gives that step — temperature, thinking, reasoning effort, the output cap, its own extra_body — and only the model, the endpoint and what you sent go out.

docs.title: What comes back
docs.text:
The result event's cv is {document, tex, pdf_base64}.

document is one flat object: what the models wrote, without the scores, with your candidate_data merged over the top. It has no schema of its own — what the template reads from it is between you and the template. Store it, edit it, and post it back to POST /v1/cv/render, which costs one LaTeX compile and no model call.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
render_document() is pure up to the compile: the document is escaped for LaTeX (including turning **bold** into \textbf{} and *italics* into \textit{}), generation_date is added — so re-rendering yesterday's file dates it today — and Jinja fills the template. The Jinja delimiters are LaTeX-safe: \VAR{}, \BLOCK{}, \#{}.

Images sent with the request are written next to the .tex under exactly the file name the part carried, because \includegraphics resolves relative to it. One pdflatex pass, not two: the shipped template has no \ref, \label or \tableofcontents, so a second pass would change nothing.

docs.title: The other three pipelines
docs.text:
None has a loop. Each runs on its own model: detect, analysis and letter.

  • jd_validator.detect — the free structural checks first (length band, no binary payload: static_jd_guess, shared with the client), and only if they pass does it cost one small model call.
  • jd_validator.analyze — extracts the posting's facts and scores it against your profile and your stated preferences. Up to three calls, the validation error fed back between them.
  • letter_generator.generate — prose in, prose out; 180–450 words, validated. The prompt asks the model to look the employer up when it can search the web; whether it can is the letter role's extra_body.

docs.title: Files and settings
docs.text:
What the 1.x pipeline reads from a protocol request: the pack files and the settings keys. Anything it does not name is ignored, cache/ included. A 0.5 server reads its own set (see the fix-0.5.x branch's CV pipeline page).

Pack file Becomes candidate_profile.json the candidate's profile (JSON object). Needed by analysis, CV, letter. candidate_data.json what the template prints: name, contact details. Needed by CV and letter. No model is shown it. candidate_preferences.md your preferences. Needed by analysis. sys_prompt_analysis.txt the analysis prompt sys_prompt_<step>.txt (jd_evaluation, profile_scoring, format_selection, cv_body, cv_duties, validation_body, validation_duties, highlight, letter, …) that prompt cv_body_schema.json, cv_duties_schema.json the JSON schema the writer is shown resume.tex.jinja the template, page counts included top-level *.png, *.jpg, *.jpeg images, under their own file name, merged over the shipped ones

Text is UTF-8 with a BOM stripped; a needed file that is missing is 400 missing_part; one that is not UTF-8, not JSON or not a JSON object is 400 bad_part. job_description.txt is decoded with undecodable bytes replaced.

Setting Means pages Page limit the CV must fit: an integer of at least 1 (default 2), else bad_part extra_body Role → JSON object: that role's request settings for this request, replacing everything models.toml gives it. Each call takes only its own roles: analysis analysis; letter letter; CV jd_evaluation, profile_scoring, format_selection, cv, duties, validation, highlight.

Unknown keys and roles are ignored.

docs.title: Running the two halves apart
docs.text: ats-strike is deliberately two programs. This page is about where to put each one, and what the boundary buys you.

docs.title: Why they are separate
docs.text:
Client Server Holds your profile, contact data, template, images, the output tree the provider API key, the prompts, the LaTeX toolchain Costs to install one file ~780 MB of TeX Live Wants to be on the machine you copy postings on wherever compute is cheap and always on Scales by being copied being given more RAM and CPU

Splitting along that line is what makes each half simple:

  • The key never leaves the server. A client needs no provider account and no .env; the one secret it can hold is a bearer token for your own server.
  • Your data never rests on the server. The profile, the contact details, the preferences and the images arrive with each request and are thrown away when it ends. There is no database, no accounts, nothing to breach beyond the requests currently in flight.
  • Nobody installs LaTeX. The toolchain, its fonts and its failure modes live in one image you did not have to reproduce on Windows.
  • Each half changes on its own. The wire format is a third package both import; tests/test_architecture.py fails the build if either side imports the other. A new client mode touches no server code, and a new model role, prompt, step or setting touches no client code: the client sends a server folder's files and its [settings] without reading them.
  • One client, several servers. The protocol knows no pipeline, so the same client talks to a 0.5, a 1.x and a 2.0 server — side by side on one posting, each from its own server folder.
flowchart LR
    subgraph c["client — your machine"]
        D["your data<br/><i>never uploaded, only sent</i>"]
    end
    subgraph w["contracts"]
        P["Envelope · StoreItem · Status · Done<br/>ServerStatus · Analysed · static_jd_guess"]
    end
    subgraph s["server — a container"]
        K["MODEL_API_KEY<br/>prompts · template · pdflatex"]
    end
    c -->|"multipart: pack · job · settings"| s
    s -->|"JSON"| c
    c -.->|imports| w
    s -.->|imports| w

docs.title: Where to run each
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph A["1 — both on your laptop"]
        A1["cv"] -->|"localhost:8080"| A2["docker run ats-strike-server"]
    end
    subgraph B["2 — server on a box you own"]
        B1["cv on 2–3 machines"] -->|"private network"| B2["one container, one work dir"]
    end
    subgraph C["3 — server on a cloud platform"]
        C1["cv anywhere"] -->|"HTTPS + bearer token"| C2["one instance<br/>scale-to-zero is fine"]
    end

1 — Both local. The default. docker run -p 8080:8080 and url = "http://localhost:8080" in the server's cv.toml section. No token needed: nothing but your own machine can reach it. This is also the cheapest way to try a different model — the container restarts in a second.

2 — Server on a machine you own. A NAS, a home server, a spare box. Set ATS_API_TOKEN even here: without it, anyone on the network can spend your provider credit. Point every client at it with url in its cv.toml server section.

3 — Server on a cloud platform. Works as-is: the image runs as any uid, needs no volume, tolerates a read-only root filesystem, and answers /healthz for the platform probe without a token. Three things to get right:

  • Set ATS_API_TOKEN and put TLS in front. The client sends your profile and your contact details in the request body.
  • One instance per ATS_WORK_DIR, and WEB_CONCURRENCY=1. A running CV job lives in the process that started it, and a starting process closes every session it finds unfinished.
  • Scale-to-zero is fine, autoscaling is not. The client knocks on /healthz three times before its first real call, so a cold start is handled — but a stream that lands on another instance than the job's only sees the job if the work root is shared, and never sees it finish if that instance is new.
  • Give the work root a home that outlives the instance — a volume, or a bucket mounted as a folder — and a session survives the instance being recycled: the client gets its CV back by running the posting again. terraform/ mounts an OSS bucket on Alibaba Cloud. A platform that only gives CPU during requests (Cloud Run's default) stalls a job whenever no stream is open: give it CPU for the whole instance instead.

docs.title: What the client needs to know
docs.text:
A [servers.<name>] section of cv.toml says it, and only folder and url are required:

[servers.v11]
folder  = "v11"            # the files this server is sent
url     = "https://ats-strike.example.run.app"
token   = "the-bearer-token"
timeout = 1800             # how long to follow one CV job

[servers.v11.settings]     # forwarded untouched; its meaning is the server's
pages = 2

That, and the protocol number /healthz reports, is the entire coupling. Everything else the client sends is content. To run a second server version beside the first, give it a section of its own in cv.toml (see the client guide).

docs.title: Keeping the boundary honest
docs.text:
If you change either half, these are the rules that keep them separable — they are also what the two repositories' test suites check:

  • client → contracts ← server → pipeline. The client and the server never import each other; the pipeline imports none of the others, and the server only its top level.
  • The contracts package imports pydantic and nothing else. It is loaded by a web server and by a frozen executable, and has to stay cheap in both.
  • No server-side dependency reaches the client: no openai, no jinja2, no pypdf, no fastapi. subprocess is allowed in exactly one file — the clipboard helper probe.
  • Anything new on the wire goes in contracts/, not in a client-side model that happens to match — and nothing pipeline-specific goes on the wire at all: a new step, artifact or setting is a file to store or a key in [settings].

docs.title: Four repositories
docs.text:
The two halves are separate repositories, each with its own version and its own release:

Repository Holds Releases ats-strike the server, the pipeline, this site the container image and the site, at the server's version ats-strike-client the CLI both executables and a data folder, at the client's version ats-strike-contract the wire format, cv_contracts nothing: the others check it out as a git submodule: at src/contracts/ here, at contracts/ in the client, the 0.5 line and ats-integration-tests ats-integration-tests the other three as submodules, and the tests that need the client and the server together nothing

A client talks to any server that speaks the same protocol number, which /healthz reports, so the two need not move in step. A wire change travels as a commit in the contract repository, then the new submodule pointer in the server and in the client, then the new pointers in ats-integration-tests: its tests/test_integration.py drives the real client against two real server apps in-process, and its CI renders a PDF with the built executable through a running server. That last step is what proves the two halves still agree.

docs.title: Developing locally, in VS Code
docs.text:
This page is for working on ats-strike itself: both halves on your own machine, under the debugger, breakpoints on either side of the HTTP call. The server is this repository and the client is ats-strike-client: check them out side by side and open both in one VS Code window. No container, no cloud instance — the client's server_url is localhost, and if you point the server at a local model endpoint too, nothing leaves the machine at all.

It is the same topology as "both on your laptop" in the deployment page, swapping docker run for uv run so you get a debugger instead of an image.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Python 3.12+, uv Builds one .venv per repository VS Code with the Python extension Ships debugpy, which the launch configs below use pdflatex on PATH Only for /v1/cv and /v1/cv/render to actually produce a PDF — see below A model endpoint Your own provider key, or a local one — see Configure

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/gcontini/ats-strike
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/gcontini/ats-strike-client
(cd ats-strike && uv sync)
(cd ats-strike-client && uv sync)

The contracts are a git submodule (the ats-strike-contract repository) in both, at src/contracts/ here and contracts/ in the client: in a clone made without --recurse-submodules it is empty until git submodule update --init, and after a git pull that moved it, git submodule update brings it along.

One .venv per checkout: the server and src/contracts/ here, contracts/ and client/ in ats-strike-client. Add both folders to one VS Code workspace (File → Add Folder to Workspace), and point each folder's Python interpreter at its own .venv/bin/python if VS Code does not pick it up on its own.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env

Fill in MODEL_API_KEY and MODEL_BASE_URL for the provider you use — see the "API keys" section of the server. cv_server loads .env itself (python-dotenv), so nothing in launch.json needs to pass it along.

Leave ATS_API_TOKEN unset. That is fine here for the same reason it is fine in deployment's scenario 1: nothing but your own machine can reach localhost:8080.

For a stack that makes no outbound network call at all, point the server at a local model server instead of a hosted provider:

MODEL_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
MODEL_API_KEY=anything   # Ollama ignores it, but the OpenAI client requires one

docs.title: The launch configs
docs.text:
Each checkout's .vscode/launch.json has its half:

Name Where Runs server (ats-strike) this repository cv_server.server:main in-process — the same entry point as uv run ats-strike, just under debugpy client (submit-raw) ats-strike-client cv submit-raw examples/posting.txt against the example candidate in that repository's examples/candidate/ — one CV, no clipboard, no confirmation prompt. The quickest way to prove the two halves talk to each other client (clipboard) ats-strike-client The interactive mode, against the same example data

and the workspace file has one compound, server + client (clipboard), that starts both. Each runs as its own debugpy session, so a breakpoint in cv_server and one in cv_client both work at the same time — they are two processes, not one call stack, so stepping through one will not show you the other side of the HTTP request.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
1. Set the Run and Debug target to server + client (clipboard) and press F5. Two debug sessions start; wait for the server's Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8080 in its Debug Console before copying a posting.
  2. Copy the text of the client repository's examples/posting.txt (or any real one). The client asks whether to submit; say y. Output lands under ats-strike-data/dev/.
  3. To check just the wiring without touching the clipboard, run client (submit-raw) on its own against an already-running server — it needs no confirmation and exits when done, which is also the one that works over an SSH or container remote with no clipboard to read.

Breakpoints in cv_server/api/ catch a request as it arrives; breakpoints in cv_client/ catch it being built or the response being parsed. curl localhost:8080/healthz works the whole time, from either a terminal or the client's own startup check.

docs.title: pdflatex, without the container
docs.text:
The image installs a specific, minimal set so the CV compiles and its icons render — see the Dockerfile at the repository root. Reproduce it on the host:

Platform What to install Debian/Ubuntu sudo apt install texlive-latex-base cm-super, then sudo resources/docker/install-fontawesome5.sh resources/docker/vendor/fontawesome5.tar.xz for the contact icons (see resources/docker/vendor/README.md) macOS A full MacTeX install already includes fontawesome5; nothing to vendor Windows MiKTeX with "install packages on the fly" on — the first compile pulls what it needs

Confirm with kpsewhich fontawesome5.sty (prints a path) and curl localhost:8080/healthz ("pdflatex": true). Without it, everything except /v1/cv and /v1/cv/render still works — /v1/jd/detect and /v1/jd/analysis never touch LaTeX.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see What to do ModuleNotFoundError: cv_client / cv_server VS Code is using a different interpreter than that folder's .venv. Reselect it, or re-run uv sync in that checkout cannot reach the ats-strike server at http://localhost:8080 The server (ats-strike) session is not running, or is still starting — check its Debug Console "status": "degraded" from /healthz No pdflatex on PATH; see above no clipboard here: neither DISPLAY nor WAYLAND_DISPLAY… apt install xclip (X11) or wl-clipboard (Wayland) locally, or a devcontainer/SSH remote with no display at all — use client (submit-raw) instead RuntimeError: ... is not set. Set it in your .env MODEL_API_KEY is empty in .env at the repository root address already in use on :8080 Something else is already listening — a leftover docker run, most likely. Stop it, or set PORT before starting the server config

docs.title: Building these pages
docs.text:
The site is doc/ rendered by MkDocs with the Material theme, configured in mkdocs.yml at the repository root. Both are pinned in the docs dependency group of pyproject.toml, so they come with the project and not from your system Python:

uv run --group docs mkdocs serve    # live preview on http://localhost:8000
uv run --group docs mkdocs build    # static HTML into out/site/ (gitignored)
Supported MkDocs 1.6+ with mkdocs-material 9.5+ Not supported MkDocs 2.0, which removes the plugin system Material is built on. Both are capped in pyproject.toml Diagrams Mermaid, as ```mermaid fences, rendered by Material through pymdownx.superfences. A different theme will print them as code Strictness strict: true — a link to a page or an anchor that does not exist fails the build

To add a page: put the Markdown in doc/ and add it to the nav: in mkdocs.yml. A page that is not in the nav still builds, but nothing links to it.

The published site is versioned. Each release deploys its own copy with mike, and the selector in the header switches between them — so the docs you are reading match the version you downloaded, not whatever main says today. Locally you still just run mkdocs; the version selector is the one thing that will not appear, because it is built from a versions.json that only exists on the published site. See Cutting a release.

docs.title: Model configurations
docs.text:
A running ledger of which provider, model and role combinations have been tried, and what happened. models.toml says what is shipped; this page says what is known to work, and why the rest does not.

Update it whenever a role changes model or provider, or a provider surprises you. An entry is only works if a real run finished and its output was used. A failure is recorded with its cause when the cause is known, and with the exact error name when it is not.

Status Meaning works A real run finished and its output was used fails It was tried and failed; the cause is in the notes unconfirmed Configured, but no run has been recorded yet

docs.title: Providers
docs.text: What each endpoint is known to accept. This is the part that carries over to the next model you try.

docs.title: Alibaba Model Studio (DashScope): Qwen and hosted DeepSeek
docs.text:
Endpoint: https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1, or the workspace endpoint of the same form shown in the console.

  • works: Chat Completions honours thinking_budget exactly. Probed on qwen3.8-max-0902 on 2026-09-28: a budget of 500 gave 500 reasoning tokens, 2000 gave 2000, both finish_reason=stop.
  • works: the switches are extra_body fields: enable_thinking, thinking_budget and enable_search.
  • works: DeepSeek V4 models served through DashScope do run web search (2026-09-27).
  • fails: the Responses API. It ignored token limits (8242 reasoning tokens against a budget of 6500) and heavy calls stalled past 600 s. ats-strike stays on Chat Completions.
  • Some models cap max_tokens at 8192; set it per model when the endpoint says so.
  • works: max_completion_tokens, which is what LangChain's ChatOpenAI sends for max_output_tokens. Probed on qwen3.8-flash on 2026-10-08: a cap of 300 with thinking_budget = 100 gave 100 reasoning tokens and 303 output tokens in all, finish_reason=length. It counts the thinking too — the old max_tokens (403 tokens out under the same test) capped the reply alone — and it must be larger than thinking_budget, or the call is a 400.
  • works: a strict json_schema for TailoredCVData, every key required and every object closed (qwen3.8-flash, 2026-10-08).

docs.title: DeepSeek (native)
docs.text:
Endpoint: https://api.deepseek.com.

  • Model ids: deepseek-flash (V4.1-Flash, current) and deepseek-v4-pro. deepseek-v4-flash is still accepted but is a retired name served by V4.1-Flash (pricing page, checked 2026-10-08).

docs.title: OpenAI
docs.text:
Endpoint: https://api.openai.com/v1.

  • gpt-6.1-terra is a valid API id: listed by /models on 2026-11-08, beside gpt-6-luna, gpt-6-sol and gpt-6.1-sol.
  • fails: gpt-6.1-terra with reasoning_effort = max (2026-11-09, Chat Completions): 400 Unsupported value: 'reasoning_effort' does not support 'max' with this model. Supported values are: 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'. Its highest is xhigh.
  • gpt-6-luna is a valid API id (released 2026-09-22) and takes reasoning_effort from none to max (OpenRouter listing).
  • fails (reported, not yet observed here): temperature other than 1 while reasoning is on. GPT-5.6-family models answer 400 Unsupported value: 'temperature' does not support 0.4 with this model (OpenAI forum); LiteLLM's Luna notes say the same for Luna. Fix: ATS_<ROLE>_TEMPERATURE=1, or empty to send none.
  • fails (expected): presence_penalty with api = "responses": the Responses API has no such parameter, and the openai SDK raises before sending (TypeError, checked offline 2026-10-08). Leave the client's presence_penalty unset for a role on the Responses API.
  • fails (expected, not yet observed here): enable_search. It is a DashScope parameter, shipped in the analysis and letter roles' extra_body. Fix: ATS_<ROLE>_EXTRA_BODY={}.
  • Do not leave thinking = "on" on an OpenAI role: it sends enable_thinking, which OpenAI does not take. Use ATS_<ROLE>_THINKING=auto.
  • Chat Completions function calling was reported to need reasoning_effort = "none". It did not on gpt-6.1-sol: adapticv-ai's validators made their replace_in_* tool calls with medium (2026-10-19). The validation role sends tools; if a model refuses them while reasoning, set its reasoning_effort to none.

docs.title: Recording a result
docs.text: Add a row under the role, with the provider, the exact model id, the settings that differ from models.toml (including any ATS_<ROLE>_* override), the date and the outcome. For a failure, the error name from the job log (provider_error: … PermissionDeniedError) or the server's own line for it (a CV's log.log carries every one) belongs in the notes; the cause belongs there once it is known. Never record keys, workspace URLs or request payloads.

docs.title: The HTTP API (protocol 2)
docs.text:
Everything is multipart/form-data in and JSON out. There is no database and no accounts: every request carries what it needs. The one thing the server keeps is a CV job's session — the events it streams — until the client says it has everything, or until it is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS.

The protocol knows no pipeline. A client sends a pack of files and stores what the server tells it to store; it never needs to know a prompt's name, a model role, a step or the analysis schema. That is what lets one client talk to a 0.5, a 1.x and a 2.0 server, side by side, on the same posting.

Base URL is wherever you run it — http://localhost:8080 by default. The interactive OpenAPI page FastAPI generates is at /docs.

The first path segment names the pipeline (/v1, /v2), and every pipeline answers the same endpoints with the same shapes; a client's server URL ends with it. Pipeline 2.0 has no job analysis and no letter: under /v2, jd/detect, jd/analysis and letter answer with v1's pipeline, so one server entry works for every command. The examples below use /v1.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Three parts, on every pipeline request.

Part Kind Holds pack file, repeatable Every file of the client's server folder, sub-folders included. The part's file name is the path relative to the server folder, with / (candidate_profile.json, cache/pool.json). job file, repeatable The posting as this server sees it: job_description.txt, analysis.json, and the files this server stored for the job before (cv.json, cv.tex, steps/...), named relative to its subfolder. A bare posting is a job with only job_description.txt. settings form field A JSON object: the settings table of the server's section in the client's cv.toml, forwarded untouched. Absent means {}.

What the files and settings mean is the pipeline's business: each server version lists what it reads in its CV pipeline page. The server only checks that they are what a request may carry, before any work: a name must be relative — no leading /, no .. part, no backslash, not empty — else 400 bad_part; more than 200 files in pack and job together is a 400 before anything is read; any one file over ATS_MAX_PART_BYTES (2 MB) is a 413; settings that is not a JSON object is a 400. A repeated name: the last one wins.

Auth. If ATS_API_TOKEN is set, every /{pipeline}/... call must send Authorization: Bearer <token>; /healthz stays open so a platform probe works. With no token set, the server is open to anyone who can reach it, which is only reasonable on a private network.

The envelope. Every response, success or failure, has the same shape:

{
  "request_id": "b510f8dff047",   // also in the X-Request-Id header
  "ok": true,
  "data": { },                    // the payload, when ok
  "error": null                   // one line, when not
}

Fields that are null are omitted.

Request ids. The server generates a 12-hex-character id per request and echoes it in the X-Request-Id header. An inbound X-Request-Id is honoured if it matches [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}. For POST /v1/cv it is the session's id, and names its directory under the work root, so anything else would be a way to write where the server was not asked to.

The protocol number. /healthz reports "protocol": 2. A server that reports none is protocol 1, and the client refuses any number but its own.

docs.title: A thing to store
docs.text:
What a server wants kept travels as one shape, whether as a CV job's store event or as an element of a REST reply's items:

{"location": "CV",                 // CV: the job folder | CACHE: <server folder>/cache
 "type": "step",                   // log: append a line | step: write a file | cv: the final PDF
 "name": "steps/key_points.json",  // relative path; empty for a log
 "text": "..."}                    // UTF-8 content — or "base64": "..." for binary (the PDF)

location and type are plain strings: a client skips a location, a type or an event name it does not know, so a server can add one without breaking an older client. Where the ats-strike client puts each one is in the client guide.

A log item's text is <ts ISO-8601 seconds, UTC> <LEVEL padded to 7> [<stage>] <message>, location CV. Token usage is a log line too: the server appends one

2026-11-13T09:46:12+00:00 INFO    [run] Σ 21 model call(s), 961.4s | input=48211, thinking=30117, output=9822

as the last log item before a CV job's done or error, and as the last item of a REST reply when the request made at least one model call.

docs.text: Method Path Auth Costs data GET /healthz no nothing ServerStatus POST /{pipeline}/jd/detect yes 0–1 small model call Detection POST /{pipeline}/jd/analysis yes 1 small model call Analysed POST /{pipeline}/cv yes minutes of model calls, a render, or nothing for a session already there 202 + CVSession GET /{pipeline}/cv/{id}/events yes nothing server-sent events DELETE /{pipeline}/cv/{id} yes nothing 200, no data DELETE /{pipeline}/cv?all yes nothing Cleanup POST /{pipeline}/cv/render yes one pdflatex run Rendered POST /{pipeline}/letter yes 1 small model call Letter

docs.title: GET /healthz
docs.text:
No auth. What this server is, which protocol it speaks, and whether it can do its job.

{"request_id": "…", "ok": true, "data": {
  "status": "ok",                 // "degraded" when pdflatex is missing
  "version": "1.1.0",
  "protocol": 2,
  "pdflatex": true,
  "models": {"detect": "deepseek-v4.1-flash", "analysis": "qwen3.8-flash",
             "letter": "qwen3.8-flash", "cv": "gpt-6.1-terra", "…": "…"},
  "auth_required": false
}}

models is the model per role. A server that serves several pipelines names each role after its pipeline: "v1.cv", "v2.compile".

docs.title: POST /v1/jd/detect
docs.text:
Is the job's job_description.txt a job posting?

curl -F job=@job_description.txt localhost:8080/v1/jd/detect

Structural checks run first — length band (ATS_JD_MIN_CHARS … _MAX_CHARS, 500–30000 by default), no binary payload — and only if they pass does it cost one small model call. The answer is {"is_job_description": true|false}; why is in the request's log, not in the reply. The same structural check ships in cv_contracts.static_jd_guess, so a client can run it before spending the call at all. No job_description.txt is a 400 missing_part; pack and settings are ignored.

docs.title: POST /v1/jd/analysis
docs.text:
Scores a posting against the candidate in the pack and extracts its facts.

curl -F job=@job_description.txt \
     -F pack=@candidate_profile.json -F pack=@candidate_preferences.md \
     localhost:8080/v1/jd/analysis

Answers {"analysis": {…}, "items": [...]}. analysis is an opaque JSON object, as the server's pipeline wrote it — each server version has its own schema. A client needs only job_title, company_name and should_apply (NO | CHECK | YES) from it, and should keep the rest as it came. items are the request's log lines, the Σ line last.

docs.title: POST /v1/cv → GET /v1/cv/{id}/events → DELETE /v1/cv/{id}
docs.text:
The expensive one. It does not wait: it starts the job as a session, which the caller follows as a stream of server-sent events and lets go of once it has stored everything.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as caller
    participant S as server
    C->>S: POST /v1/cv (pack, job, settings)<br/>X-Request-Id: the session id
    S-->>C: 202 {reattached: false}
    C->>S: GET /v1/cv/{id}/events
    loop while the job runs
        S-->>C: status · store
    end
    S-->>C: done {detail} — and the stream closes
    Note over C: has stored every item
    C->>S: DELETE /v1/cv/{id}
    S-->>C: 200
ID=$(sha256sum job_description.txt | cut -c1-64)
curl -s -H "X-Request-Id: $ID" -F job=@job_description.txt \
     -F pack=@candidate_profile.json -F pack=@candidate_data.json \
     -F settings='{"pages": 2}' localhost:8080/v1/cv
curl -sN localhost:8080/v1/cv/$ID/events      # the job, to its last event
curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8080/v1/cv/$ID    # once everything is stored

docs.title: POST /v1/cv
docs.text:
What a CV request does is decided by the job, the same way on every server version:

  1. the job holds cv.json → it is rendered (the document wins over the tex);
  2. else it holds cv.tex → it is compiled as it stands;
  3. else the CV is written from job_description.txt.

There is no step-level resume: a job that holds only steps/... is written again. A written CV stores step cv.json (the merged document, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), step cv.tex, and cv cv.pdf; the 1.x pipeline also stores each intermediate result as step steps/<name>.json as it is ready, the 2.0 pipeline its job's steps as steps/<name>.json and steps/<name>.md. A rendered document stores step cv.tex and cv cv.pdf; a compiled tex stores cv cv.pdf only.

The 2.0 pipeline's store (/v2/cv) is built once per profile and travels as CACHE step items: items.json, tree.json and pool.json, each stored as soon as it is built, with its readable page (items.md, tree.md, pool.md, review.md). The client keeps them in the server folder's cache/, and every pack sends them back (cache/items.json, ...); the pipeline builds only the files the pack lacks, in that order. Nothing checks the store against the profile: after a profile change, delete cache/. No other pipeline stores a CACHE item.

Answers 202 with {"request_id": "<id>", "ok": true, "data": {"reattached": false}}.

The session id is the caller's. Send it as X-Request-Id. The client uses the SHA-256 of the job's job_description.txt, so running the same posting again finds the session it already has, and a client that died, or lost its connection, loses nothing it paid for. When the id already has a session, nothing is started — no slot is claimed either — and the answer says "reattached": true: follow its events as for a new one. Sessions whose last event is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS (1 by default) are deleted first, so an old one is not found. With no X-Request-Id, the server picks an id and every POST is a new job. 429 too_many_jobs applies to a new job only.

A pack problem the job finds once it runs — a missing candidate_data.json, say — ends the session with an error event carrying 400, not a synchronous 400.

docs.title: GET /v1/cv/{id}/events
docs.text:
text/event-stream. Every event the session has — from the first, or from the one after Last-Event-ID: n — then each new one as the job writes it, until the last, after which the stream closes. A : ping line every 15 quiet seconds keeps the connection open through a long model call. The session is files, so a stream can be opened as often as you like, while the job runs or long after, and a dropped one loses nothing: reconnect with the last id: you got.

id: 1
event: status
data: {"status": "started", "detail": ""}

id: 2
event: status
data: {"status": "jd_evaluation", "detail": ""}

id: 3
event: store
data: {"location": "CV", "type": "log", "name": "", "text": "2026-11-13T09:30:53+00:00 INFO    [cv.jd_evaluation]   ⏱ [jd_evaluation] deepseek-flash 21.2s | input=1847, thinking=7256, output=832"}

id: 4
event: store
data: {"location": "CV", "type": "step", "name": "steps/key_points.json", "text": "[\n  {\n    \"id\": 1, …"}

id: 5
event: status
data: {"status": "profile_scoring", "detail": "11 key points, tokens used=9935, thinking=7256, elapsed=21.3s"}

id: 96
event: store
data: {"location": "CV", "type": "cv", "name": "cv.pdf", "base64": "JVBERi0…"}

id: 97
event: store
data: {"location": "CV", "type": "log", "name": "", "text": "… INFO    [run] Σ 21 model call(s), 961.4s | input=…, thinking=…, output=…"}

id: 98
event: done
data: {"detail": "done, 21 model calls, 2 page(s)"}
Event Payload Notes status Status: status (free text), detail Shown, never stored. The first event of every session is status: "started". An identical consecutive status is not repeated. store StoreItem Each step result as it is ready, each log line as it is logged, then the CV. done Done: detail The last event. detail is the pipeline's one-line summary. error Failure: http_status, error The last event.

status and detail are written for a person, in the pipeline's own words. A failed job reports itself here, with the status its cause maps to (400, 422, 502, 504) and the cause in the same form as any other error; the Σ line before it still says what the run cost. A job the server restarted under ends with 503 unavailable. See the CV pipeline for what each step of this server's pipeline does.

404 unknown_request means there is no session by that id: it was acknowledged, it is older than the server keeps sessions, or it never started.

docs.title: DELETE /v1/cv/{id}
docs.text: Acknowledge: the caller has everything, and the server deletes the session. Do it once every item is stored, not before — until then the session is what lets a caller that died get its CV back for nothing. 409 job_not_ready while the job runs: its worker is still writing there, and a new session for the same posting would be the same directory. 404 when there is no such session.

docs.title: DELETE /v1/cv?all
docs.text: Deletes every session whose job is not running, and answers {"deleted": 3, "running": 1}. Without all it is a 400: not something to do by accident.

docs.title: POST /v1/cv/render
docs.text:
The CV request minus the writing: the job's cv.json rendered, or its cv.tex compiled, with the pack's template and images. With neither file it is a 400 missing_part; with both, the document wins.

curl -F job=@cv.json -F pack=@resume.tex.jinja localhost:8080/v1/cv/render
curl -F job=@cv_edited.tex\;filename=cv.tex     localhost:8080/v1/cv/render

Answers {"items": [...]}: the same items a CV request would store. Cheap and deterministic: editing the content and rendering again never costs a model call. The rendered .tex is dated at render time, so rendering yesterday's document dates it today.

docs.title: POST /v1/letter
docs.text:
curl -F job=@job_description.txt -F job=@analysis.json \
     -F pack=@candidate_profile.json -F pack=@candidate_data.json \
     localhost:8080/v1/letter

Answers {"text": "…", "items": [...]}. The job's analysis.json is optional and makes the letter more targeted (on 1.x it also enables the web research when the endpoint supports it).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A failed request returns the same envelope with ok: false and one line saying what went wrong, its kind and its stage — one line, except that a failed compile adds the end of the TeX log on the lines after it, because only the TeX log says where the document breaks:

{"request_id": "b510f8dff047", "ok": false,
 "error": "model_output [cv.profile_scoring]: profile_scoring: no usable reply in 3 attempts:\n- it is not a JSON list"}
Status Kind Means 400 bad_request, missing_part, bad_part A needed file is absent, empty, not UTF-8, not JSON, not an object; a name is unusable; too many files; settings is not an object 401 unauthorized ATS_API_TOKEN is set and the request had no matching token. Answers with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer 404 unknown_request No CV session by that id: acknowledged, older than the server keeps sessions, or never started 409 job_not_ready The CV job is still running, so its session cannot be acknowledged yet 413 part_too_large A file exceeded ATS_MAX_PART_BYTES 422 latex_compile The template or the .tex does not compile. The end of the TeX log follows the error line 429 too_many_jobs All job slots are busy. Answers with Retry-After: 30 502 any other pipeline kind (model_output, provider_error, provider_unreachable, …) The model never produced usable output, or its endpoint failed. An endpoint's body is never echoed — it can carry the endpoint and the key 504 latex_timeout, provider_timeout A compile or the provider hit its timeout 500 internal_error A bug here. Everything else above is an answer, not a crash

The stage in brackets ([cv.profile_scoring], [compile], [render]) says where in the pipeline it happened. For a CV job, the attempts that led there — every failed one included, with its token cost — are in the session's log items. For any other request, the reply's items carry its log lines; the server's own log (stdout) has every line under the request id.

docs.title: The wire format as a package
docs.text:
cv_contracts is the same set of pydantic models the server answers with, published as its own package so a client can import it instead of hand-rolling the shapes:

from cv_contracts import (
    PROTOCOL, Envelope, ServerStatus, Detection, Analysed, Rendered, Letter,
    EVENT_PAYLOADS, TERMINAL_EVENTS, StoreItem, Status, Done, Failure,
    CVSession, Cleanup, static_jd_guess,
)

envelope = Envelope[Rendered].model_validate(response.json())
pdf = next(i for i in envelope.data.items if i.type == "cv").content()   # bytes

item = EVENT_PAYLOADS["store"].model_validate_json(data)   # a store event's data

It depends on pydantic and nothing else, and knows no pipeline: no prompt names, no model roles, no step names, no analysis schema.

docs.title: Cutting a release
docs.text:
One version for the server, and one thing you type. Actions → Release → Run workflow → 0.3.0 → Run. Nothing happens on your machine.

.github/workflows/release.yml writes that number into the pipeline's and the server's pyproject.toml and uv.lock, commits it, tags v0.3.0, and builds everything from that tag: the server image on Docker Hub and Alibaba, this site under its own version, and a release page with the notes.

The client is not part of it: it lives in ats-strike-client, has its own version, and its own Release workflow publishes the executables — see its release page. A client talks to any server with the same protocol number, so the two are released whenever each is ready.

docs.title: Before the first one
docs.text:
Four repository secrets and one variable, set once under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

Name Kind What it is DOCKERHUB_USERNAME secret The Docker Hub account that owns lmstch/ats-strike. DOCKERHUB_TOKEN secret An access token for it, not the account password. ACR_REPOSITORY variable The Alibaba Container Registry repository Function Compute deploys from: terraform output -raw push_repository in terraform/. ACR_USERNAME secret Its registry username, from the console's Access Credentials page. ACR_PASSWORD secret Its fixed registry password. An AccessKey does not work.

Without them the image job fails at docker login, after the image has been built and checked — and because release waits on every job, no release page is published until they exist. terraform/README.md covers the Alibaba side.

GitHub Pages, once, under Settings → Pages: source GitHub Actions. Not Deploy from a branch — gh-pages is still where every version is kept, but the docs job uploads that branch and deploys it itself. Choosing the branch instead hands publishing to the build Pages runs on a push, and that build never fires here: mike pushes as github-actions[bot], and a GITHUB_TOKEN push starts no workflow run. The branch would move and the site would not. Nothing else writes that branch — it belongs to mike.

One consequence worth knowing: with this source, pushing gh-pages by hand publishes nothing. A mike deploy --push from a laptop updates the store and leaves the site where it was. Releasing is what publishes.

The workflow also declares permissions: contents: write. The repository default for GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only, and this workflow pushes a commit, a tag and a release; without that block the push is refused with a 403. The docs job asks for two more of its own — pages: write and id-token: write — because it deploys the site rather than leaving that to a branch build.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Type the number bare: 0.3.0, not v0.3.0. The tag gets the v.

It refuses, before writing anything, when:

Refusal Why the version is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH the tag and the image tag are both built from it you dispatched from a branch other than main a release that is not on the main line is a release nobody can reconstruct v<version> is already on the remote re-releasing a version silently is how two different images end up with one number

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    TAG["<b>tag</b><br/>validate · rewrite two pyprojects<br/>uv lock · commit · tag · push --atomic"]
    IMG["<b>image</b><br/>DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 docker build<br/>assert /healthz version<br/>docker push Docker Hub :x.y.z and :latest<br/>docker push Alibaba :x.y.z"]
    DOC["<b>docs</b><br/>mike deploy x.y.z latest<br/>mike set-default latest<br/>→ gh-pages → deploy-pages"]
    REL["<b>release</b><br/>gh release create<br/>notes, no assets"]
    TAG --> IMG --> REL
    TAG --> DOC --> REL

The tag is pushed first, before anything is built. That order is forced: the image has to carry the version, so the bump has to precede the build, and the build jobs can only check out a commit that exists on the remote. Every "tag last" arrangement ends up shipping the bump as a patch and re-applying it in each job — more moving parts for the same result.

release waits for every other job, so the release page never announces a version whose server image is not on Docker Hub or whose docs are not up. The image job logs in to the registry after the build and the health check, so a broken image never gets as far as authenticating.

docs.title: Where the version lives
docs.text:
There is no __version__ string in the source to forget to bump. One number is written in one place and everything else reads it:

Where Who writes it pyproject.toml the workflow, with sed uv.lock uv lock, in the same commit /healthz and the OpenAPI document importlib.metadata.version("ats-strike-server")

src/contracts/ is not: it is the ats-strike-contract submodule and keeps its own version there. A release ships whatever commit the submodule points at.

uv.lock is in that list because it records the project's version as well. A bump that did not regenerate it would commit a lock that disagrees with the manifest, which uv lock --check and uv sync --locked both refuse. The image itself would still be right — it installs the project from source, so the manifest wins — but a repository whose lock contradicts its manifest is a trap for the next person.

What guards the version in the image is not the lock but the assertion: the image job reads /healthz from the container it just built, before it is published.

docs.title: What gets published
docs.text: Artifact Where Name the release notes the release page vx.y.z, no assets: the executables are on ats-strike-client's own release pages the server image Docker Hub lmstch/ats-strike:x.y.z and :latest the same image, for Function Compute Alibaba Container Registry <ACR_REPOSITORY>:x.y.z, deployed by terraform apply this site GitHub Pages, from gh-pages /x.y.z/, and /latest/ which / redirects to

docs.title: The site's own versions
docs.text:
mike keeps one built copy of doc/ per release on the gh-pages branch, plus a versions.json that the selector in the header reads:

gh-pages/
├── 0.2.0/           one full site per release
├── 0.3.0/
├── latest/          an alias, moved by --update-aliases
├── versions.json    what the selector offers
└── index.html       redirects / to latest/

The docs version is the release version, in full — 0.3.0, not 0.3. mike's own convention is major.minor, so that patches share a docs version, but one number for the whole server is worth more here than a shorter selector: a tag, an image tag and a docs URL that all read 0.3.0 need no explaining.

mike set-default --push latest runs on every release. It is idempotent, and doing it every time is what lets the first release set the redirect up with no manual step.

Locally, mkdocs serve and mkdocs build are unchanged and unversioned. The selector is built at runtime from a versions.json that only the published site has, so it will not appear in a local preview — that is expected, not a misconfiguration.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
What failed What is left behind What to do tag nothing — the branch and the tag are pushed with --atomic, so they land together or not at all fix it and dispatch again a later job, transiently — a runner flake, a registry 5xx the bump commit and the tag, no release Re-run failed jobs. tag is skipped and its sha output carries over, so the re-run builds the same commit. a later job, for a real reason — the image fails its health check, a doc link is dead the same the release was never valid. Fix it on main and release the next patch number.

docs and image both publish before release does, so a failure after them can leave a site and an image for a version that has no release page. Both are safe to redo: mike deploy overwrites the version's directory, and docker push overwrites the tag.

The last row is the one that looks wrong and is not. Tags are free, a skipped patch number costs nothing, and the alternative — teaching the workflow to delete and re-push its own tag — is a feature nobody asked for that can destroy a good release.

One thing worth knowing: the release commit does not run CI. Pushes made with GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger further workflow runs. Its only difference from main is two version strings and the lock, and both uv sync --frozen and the Docker build fail loudly on a broken lock — but the rule that follows from it is: release only from a green main.

docs.title: ats-strike server
docs.text:
The compute half of ats-strike: it turns a job description into tailored CV data, compiles LaTeX into a PDF, analyses postings and writes cover letters.

It holds your provider API keys and a set of default prompts. Everything else — your profile, your contact details, your preferences, your images — arrives with each request, as the pack of files the client sends from its server folder, and is thrown away when it ends. There is no database and no user accounts.

It is two packages: cv_server speaks protocol 2 — request reading, auth, sessions, the event stream — and pipeline_v1 makes the CV. The protocol knows no prompt, role or step, so the same cv_server runs in front of every pipeline version, and one client can use a 0.5 and a 1.x server side by side.

It does keep one thing, on the filesystem: a session per CV job under ATS_WORK_DIR — every event the job wrote, its finished PDF included. Writing a CV takes minutes, so POST /v1/cv answers immediately and the client follows the session as it grows. It waits there until the client says it has everything, or until it is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
docker build -t ats-strike-server .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env ats-strike-server
curl localhost:8080/healthz

Or, from a checkout:

uv sync
uv run ats-strike

The image is ~780 MB, almost all of it the LaTeX toolchain. It runs as any uid, needs no volume, and works with a read-only root filesystem as long as /tmp is writable (docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:exec). exec on that tmpfs is required: pdflatex writes and then reads back its font cache there. A tmpfs also means a session does not survive a restart — mount a volume, or a bucket, at ATS_WORK_DIR if you want it to.

docker compose up --build from this directory does the same with the settings below already wired.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
The server calls one model per job. The endpoint is declared once, in the [provider] table of resources/models.toml; the key itself comes from the environment. A role that sets use_alternate_provider = 2 calls a second endpoint instead — as shipped, the six steps of a CV, on DeepSeek's own API:

MODEL_API_KEY=sk-...
MODEL_BASE_URL=https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1
MODEL_API_KEY2=sk-...
MODEL_BASE_URL2=https://api.deepseek.com

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works — OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, a local Ollama. Switching providers is just replacing those two values in .env; models.toml's [provider] table names the same two variables and doesn't need to change.

Role What it does Shipped as detect JD detection, a one-word YES/NO deepseek-flash (provider 2), thinking off, 1000 max output tokens analysis JD analysis gpt-6-luna (provider 3), Responses API, pro mode, xhigh effort letter Cover letters gpt-6-luna (provider 3), xhigh effort jd_evaluation A CV's key points, from the posting deepseek-flash (provider 2), medium effort profile_scoring Your profile scored against them, one list at a time the same, high effort format_selection The CV format, the experiences and their duties the same, medium effort cv Writing the CV body, and each experience on its own the same, medium effort validation Checking them against your profile, as replacements the same, medium effort highlight The **bold**/*italic* keyword pass the same, medium effort

See the CV pipeline for what the six steps do.

Each key of a role — model, model_provider (standard or deepseek), api (chat_completions or responses), structured_output, temperature, thinking, reasoning_effort, max_output_tokens, extra_body and use_alternate_provider — can also be overridden with an env var, without editing models.toml. Handy for a Docker deployment:

ATS_V1_CV_MODEL=qwen-max
ATS_V1_CV_TEMPERATURE=0.2
ATS_V1_CV_API=responses
ATS_V1_CV_EXTRA_BODY={"thinking_budget": 4000}
ATS_V1_CV_USE_ALTERNATE_PROVIDER=2
ATS_V1_LETTER_EXTRA_BODY={}

EXTRA_BODY is JSON and replaces the whole table: it carries what only one provider understands, such as DashScope's thinking_budget and enable_search. An empty value drops a key, as if models.toml never declared it — an empty TEMPERATURE sends none, for an endpoint that rejects one (OpenAI's reasoning models). Nothing checks that a combination suits your endpoint; the comments in models.toml list the known traps.

The pattern is ATS_V1_<ROLE>_<FIELD> (ATS_V2_… for pipeline 2.0) for DETECT, ANALYSIS, LETTER, JD_EVALUATION, PROFILE_SCORING, FORMAT_SELECTION, CV (the body), DUTIES (the experiences), VALIDATION and HIGHLIGHT; see .env.example. A request can do the same for one call with extra_body.<role> in its settings, which replaces every setting of that role.

Model calls go through LangChain. Setting LANGSMITH_TRACING sends every prompt — your profile included — to LangSmith; leave it unset unless you mean to.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Variable Default What it does PORT / HOST 8080 / 0.0.0.0 Where uvicorn listens WEB_CONCURRENCY 1 uvicorn worker processes ATS_API_TOKEN unset Bearer token clients must send. Unset means no auth. ATS_RESOURCES baked in Directory of replacement prompts/template/models.toml, one sub-folder per pipeline (v1/) ATS_WORK_DIR system temp Where CV sessions are kept, one directory of events each, under a directory per pipeline (v1/, v2/) ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS 1 Days a session nobody acknowledged is kept after its last event ATS_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS 10 Requests in flight; the rest get 429 ATS_LATEX_TIMEOUT 120 Seconds before a compile is killed (read by the pipeline) ATS_MAX_PART_BYTES 2000000 Cap on any one uploaded file ATS_JD_MIN_CHARS / _MAX_CHARS 500 / 30000 Length band for the free JD check ATS_LOG_LEVEL INFO Logging level

docs.title: Prompts and the template
docs.text:
The prompts, the two JSON schemas the CV writer is shown and resume.tex.jinja ship inside the image (resources/v1/). To change them permanently, mount a directory with your versions and set ATS_RESOURCES to it; v1 reads its files from its v1/ sub-folder, laid out as resources/v1:

$ATS_RESOURCES/
└── v1/
    ├── sys_prompt_cv_body.txt
    ├── resume.tex.jinja
    └── models.toml

Anything missing there falls back to the built-in copy, the highlight prompt (sys_prompt_highlight.txt) included: each pipeline ships its own. To change any of them for one request, send them in the pack — that is what the client does with every file in its server folder.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text: Set ATS_API_TOKEN and every /v1/... call must send Authorization: Bearer <token>. /healthz stays open so a platform probe works. With no token set the server is open to anyone who can reach it, which is only reasonable on a private network.

docs.title: The API
docs.text:
The full specification is in doc/protocol.md. In short: every pipeline request is multipart/form-data with the same three parts — pack (the client's server folder, each file named by its relative path), job (job_description.txt, analysis.json, and what this server stored for the job before) and settings (a JSON object, forwarded untouched) — and every response is the same envelope:

{
  "request_id": "b510f8dff047",   // also in the X-Request-Id header
  "ok": true,
  "data": { },                    // the payload, when ok
  "error": null                   // set when ok is false
}

A failed request returns the same body with ok: false and error set to one line saying what went wrong, its kind and its stage:

{"request_id": "b510f8dff047", "ok": false,
 "error": "model_output [cv.profile_scoring]: profile_scoring: no usable reply in 3 attempts:\n- it is not a JSON list"}

What the server wants the client to keep — a step's result, a log line, the PDF — comes back as things to store, {location, type, name, text|base64}: as a CV session's store events, and as a REST reply's items. Token usage is a log line: the last one of a reply or a session adds up the model calls.

Call What it does GET /healthz No auth. The version, "protocol": 2, whether pdflatex is present, the model per role, whether a token is required POST /v1/jd/detect Is the job's job_description.txt a posting? Structural checks, then one small model call POST /v1/jd/analysis Scores the posting against the pack's profile and preferences; answers {analysis, items}, the analysis an opaque object POST /v1/cv 202, and the CV job starts as a session keyed by X-Request-Id: the job's cv.json is rendered, else its cv.tex compiled, else the CV is written — minutes of model calls in six steps, then a render cut to the page limit GET /v1/cv/{id}/events The session as server-sent events — status, store, then done or error — replayable from Last-Event-ID DELETE /v1/cv/{id} The client has stored everything: the session is deleted (409 while running) DELETE /v1/cv?all Every session not running, deleted POST /v1/cv/render The job's cv.json rendered or cv.tex compiled: no model call POST /v1/letter A cover letter: {text, items} 
ID=$(sha256sum job_description.txt | cut -c1-64)
curl -s -H "X-Request-Id: $ID" -F job=@job_description.txt \
     -F pack=@candidate_profile.json -F pack=@candidate_data.json localhost:8080/v1/cv
curl -sN localhost:8080/v1/cv/$ID/events      # the job, to its last event
curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8080/v1/cv/$ID    # once everything is saved

Why the CV needs candidate_data.json, and the template. The page limit is enforced by actually compiling the CV and counting its pages, removing duties until it fits. A page count taken with a different template, or with the contact block missing, is not the page count of the CV you will send. No model is shown candidate_data.json: it goes to the renderer and nowhere else.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
A CV job runs for minutes after the request that started it has been answered. That is the one thing to plan around.

  • ATS_WORK_DIR is state. Every CV session lives there until the client acknowledges it or it outlives ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS. The default is the system temp directory, which on most container platforms is RAM-backed and empty again after a redeploy. Mount a volume — or a bucket, as the Alibaba deployment in terraform/ does — to have sessions outlive the instance. Each event is a file written once, which is what a bucket mounted as a folder can do; LaTeX's scratch space stays on local disk.
  • One process per work root. WEB_CONCURRENCY=1. The job slots and the worker threads are per-process, and a starting process ends every session that has not ended with a 503 — which is right for its own orphans and wrong for a sibling's live jobs.
  • A stream lasts as long as its job. Every other call returns in seconds; only /v1/cv/render waits on a compile. A CV's event stream stays open for the minutes the job takes, pinging every 15 s, so a platform request timeout has to outlast the longest job — the client reconnects after a cut, but some platforms restart the instance on a timeout.
  • Concurrency. Ten jobs in flight is the default; each is mostly idle waiting on the provider, but each also compiles LaTeX several times. Size memory and CPU for the compiles, not the waiting. Beyond the limit the server answers 429 with Retry-After immediately rather than queueing a caller for minutes.
  • Scaling. A running job lives in the instance that started it. Run one instance; with a shared work root, any instance can replay a finished session, but only one may start up and close orphans at a time.
  • Cold starts build an HTTP client per model role and read the prompts. It is fast, but the first request also has to warm the LaTeX font cache in /tmp.

docs.title: Sandboxing
docs.text: A request may supply the LaTeX template, and /v1/cv/render accepts a whole .tex. That is arbitrary LaTeX, so every compile runs with shell escape disabled (-no-shell-escape, shell_escape=f), reads and writes confined to the scratch directory (openin_any=p, openout_any=p), no stdin to block on, a timeout, and its own HOME/TEXMFVAR. The scratch directory is deleted when the request ends. Error responses have the scratch path scrubbed out of the LaTeX log before it goes back.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see What it means 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer ATS_API_TOKEN is set on the server and the request had no matching token 413 A file exceeded ATS_MAX_PART_BYTES 422 latex_compile [compile] The template or the .tex does not compile. The end of the TeX log follows the error line and says where 429 with Retry-After All job slots are busy — retry, or raise ATS_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS 502 model_output [cv.<step>] in an error event The job failed: the model never produced valid output. The session's log items show each failed attempt and its cost 404 unknown_request No CV session by that id: acknowledged, expired, or never started 409 job_not_ready from DELETE /v1/cv/{id} The job is still running; acknowledge it once its last event is in 504 The compile, or the whole run, hit its timeout "status": "degraded" on /healthz No pdflatex on PATH — CV and render calls will fail

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run pytest tests/server tests/pipeline_v1   # no API key, no network
uv run pytest                                  # every package, plus the integration test

The LaTeX-dependent tests skip themselves when pdflatex is absent. Nothing in the suite calls a model. tests/server run the protocol against a stub pipeline; tests/pipeline_v1/pipeline_helpers.py wires a real ModelSelector to a fake HTTP transport, so request assembly, structured output, retries and usage logging are all the production code paths — and the integration test runs two real servers on it.

The layout is described in src/cv_server/__init__.py and src/pipeline_v1/__init__.py; the rules the code follows are in AGENTS.md at the repository root.
